newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's unemployment rate shows significant drop.
newsitem.headline: Canada's unemployment rate shows significant drop.

text.p: The weak link in Canada's economy -- the job market -- finally showed signs of strength on Friday as the June unemployment rate fell to 9.1 percent, the lowest rate since September 1995.
Despite months of healthy indicators in other areas of the economy, Canada's unemployment rate had stuck stubbornly around 10 percent for years.
The June employment report released on Friday by Statistics Canada, the government statistics agency, at last showed growth in Canada's job market, economists said.

"This economy has had one foot on the accelerator in terms of (low) interest rates, and one foot on the brakes in terms of job losses in the public sector," said John Clinkard, senior economist at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
Job creation rose 51,500 during the month, bringing the total number of jobs in Canada to 13.95 million.

"This is the final piece of the puzzle and it's fitting into place quite nicely," said David Rosenberg, senior economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns in Toronto. "I think the word 'tremendous' is an understatement."
The report invigorated the Canadian dollar, pushing it to 73.05 U.S. cents at the market opening on Friday from Thursday's close of 72.82 U.S. cents.
The number of full-time jobs surged, rising 93,700 from the month before, but part-time employment fell by 42,200, Statistics Canada said in its jobs report .

Private sector employment, excluding self-employed people, expanded by 57,000 or 0.6 percent in June, while public sector employment dropped 25,000 or 1.2 percent. Self-employment continuted to expand, rising 19,000 or 0.8 percent.
The private sector was finally able to offset a long trend of job losses in the public sector, economists said.
Most of the job gains in June were in the manufacturing sector, Statistics Canada said.

Youth unemployment remained a problem. The unemployment rate for Canadian young people rose 0.3 percentage points to 17.5 percent as more people joined the labor force in search of work, StatsCan said.
But job creation in the rest of the population was strong enough that it would eventually trickle down to unemployed youth, economists said.
In the past four months, about 235,000 full-time jobs were created, Statistics Canada said.
"We're packing a powerful punch here," said Rosenberg, who observed that job creation in the past four months was more than employment growth in the previous 28 months combined.
He said the strength in the job market might prompt the Bank of Canada to tighten monetary conditions "sooner rather than later."

But CIBC's Clinkard said, however, that the central bank might remain neutral as there were no signs of inflationary pressure in Canada. He predicted the unemployment rate would drop below nine percent by the end of the year.
